newsitem.title: SPAIN: Half million Spaniards protest against ETA kidnap.
newsitem.headline: Half million Spaniards protest against ETA kidnap.

text.p: Half a million Spaniards led by Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar marched in protest here on Saturday against a threat by ETA Basque guerrillas to kill a kidnapped politician.
Chanting "life yes, ETA no", they flocked through the northern Basque city in what officals said was the biggest protest against ETA separatist rebels in history.

The demonstration, estimated by police at half a million strong, started at 12 noon (1000 GMT) -- just four hours before a deadline set by ETA to kill Miguel Angel Blanco, a young town councillor from the ruling Popular Party.
The group kidnapped Blanco on Thursday and said they would kill him unless the government gave in to its ultimatum to move some 500 ETA inmates to prisons in the Basque country by 4 p.m. on Saturday.
The kidnapping and death threat caused outrage across Spain, which had just been celebrating the release of two other ETA hostages last week, and sparked an angry backlash.
Even nationalist politicians in the region who support the separatist cause but oppose violence turned out for the protest and called on ETA to release Blanco.

"They (ETA) have to know we cannot live with this barbarity any longer. If they carry out this threat, the Basque people will never, never forgive them," Basque interior counsellor Juan Maria Atutxa told state television in Bilbao.

Aznar headed the protest march in Bilbao marching alongside his wife and fierce Basque nationalist leader Jose Antonio Ardanza. They carried a yellow banner at the front that said "Peace Now and Forever" in the Basque language.
The protest drew people from all over Spain, but mostly from the Basque region where special buses and trains were arranged to transport thousands of visitors to Bilbao.

All of Spain's main television stations aired the nearly three-hour demonstration live, showing aerial views of Bilbao's packed streets and plazas with a sea of marchers stretching on for kilometres (miles).
"This shows the solidarity of the Basques against ETA, they are more isolated than ever," Bilbao resident Marcelino Oreja said.
"Today we are not talking about ideology, we are talking about something sweeter, we are talking about liberty."
Grim-faced protesters held up their hands in a stop signal and shouted "Enough, already" and "Freedom, freedom".
ETA has killed some 800 people since starting a drive for Basque independence in 1968.
Herri Batasuna, ETA's political wing, consistently gets about 15 percent of the vote in the region, but Basques have become increasingly disgusted with the ongoing violence.
A peace movement started about five years ago in the region has encouraged Basques to overcome the fear of publicly defying ETA and take an active role in trying to stop the killings.
The mass march on Saturday ended in front of Bilbao's town hall where the protesters held a five-minute period of silence before hearing a statement from the family of the 29-year-old kidnap victim.

"Life is a right for everyone," Blanco's sister told the demonstration to enormous applause. "We are living in very difficult times, it's a very anxious wait, but we have not lost hope...we want to thank the people of the Basque region and all of Spain for the affection they have shown us."
